analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes and in-home care providers from forcing residents into pre-dispute arbitration agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 7 cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes and home care providers often require residents or their families to sign arbitration agreements at admission, which means that if the resident is later neglected or abused, the family must take the case to a private arbitrator instead of a jury, with no public record and no appeal. This bill would make such pre-dispute agreements invalid for anyone in Medicare or Medicaid nursing facilities, home- and community-based services, or home health care, including agreements already signed.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and people receiving home care, plus their families, who would regain the right to take injury and neglect cases to open court instead of private arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home and home care residents

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements between Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities and their residents, and makes them unenforceable regardless of whether the agreement was signed before or after the law takes effect.
It applies the same prohibition to home- and community-based services and home health care providers, covering the person receiving care and any affiliate or agent of the provider.
It requires a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether the law applies to a given agreement, keeping the question out of the arbitration system itself.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home chains and long-term care providers, who would face injury lawsuits in open court, with publicly available verdicts and potentially larger awards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home and long-term care providers

drawbacks.text: Providers argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than litigation, and that resolving disputes privately can avoid drawn-out court cases for families.
The bill applies to agreements signed before enactment, wiping out existing contracts with current and former residents, which goes beyond stopping future mandatory arbitration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to residents is concrete: a jury trial with a public record is the main check on negligent facilities, and arbitration clauses signed at admission often come with little explanation to frail or cognitively impaired residents. The cost falls on providers through litigation exposure, which is the point of the bill, though the retroactive reach into already-signed agreements is the strongest honest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and subcommittees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky as an original cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to their health and Social Security subcommittees.
Seven additional Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no further action was recorded after the subcommittee referrals in April 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home chains and long-term care providers keep the ability to enforce pre-dispute arbitration agreements, keeping resident injury disputes out of open court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home and long-term care providers

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no chamber ever voted on the bill, so the vote divide was never tested; the bill died in committee with only 8 total supporters.

industries.industry: Nursing home chains and long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill would strip their ability to route resident injury and neglect disputes into private arbitration, exposing them to public jury trials. Their interest in keeping the current system is directly at odds with residents' access to court.

industries.industry: Home health and home care agencies
industries.note: Home- and community-based and home health providers would face the same ban, so workers' and patients' injury claims could go to court. Their current arbitration shield would disappear.
Private arbitration firms would lose a large stream of long-term care disputes, which the bill would return to the court system.
